scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Emerging from 19th-century Tobagonian funeral wakes, the limbo symbolizes the cycle of life and death, with the dancer's emergence from beneath the bar representing a triumph over the grave.
This is Limbo (dance). 19th century-present.
on_screen: Title card: Limbo (dance) · Trinidad and Tobago · 19th century-present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Originating in 19th-century Tobago, the limbo was traditionally performed at wakes.
It is believed to be related to African legba or legua games and reflects the cycle of life.
It was popularized in the 1950s by Julia Edwards.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used at funeral wakes to symbolize the triumph of life over death.
In modern contexts, it is used as a social icebreaker at resorts and during Carnival.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: “ JAMAICA ” 1974 TOURISM FILM w/ RAGGAE LEGEND BYRON LEE PORT ROYAL SCUBA DIVING 51304 (https://archive.org/details/51304-jamaica)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Contestants pass under a horizontal bar with their backs facing the floor.
Players must bend backwards without touching the bar or the floor with their hands.
The bar is lowered after each round until only one player remains.
Watch for The Arch.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Single-file line passing under a horizontal bar.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performances typically respond to Afro-Caribbean drum patterns.
Popular music associated with the dance includes 'Limbo Rock' by Chubby Checker and 'Limbo Break' by Brigo.
Listen for the drums.
Characterized by driving Afro-Caribbean percussion rhythms that provide a steady pulse for the dancer's movements.
